source_text: γενέσθαι οὐρανόν, γῆν, θάλατταν ἐπιφερόμενον ἐπὶ τοῦ ὕδατος καὶ ζωογόνον καὶ ζωοτρόφον αὐτὸ ἀπεργαζόμενον; ὥσπερ γὰρ διὰ τὸ λέγειν ἐν τῷ Ἰὼβ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ· «ὁ τανύσας τὸν οὐρανὸν μόνος,» οὐκ ἀφιστᾷ μὲν τῆς δημιουργίας τὸν ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα καὶ ἐν ᾧ πάντα συνέστηκεν πατέρα πῶς γὰρ ἂν εἴη λοιπὸν ταῦτα ἀληθῆ;, οὕτως οὐδὲ τὸ τῆς σοφίας καὶ δυνάμεως καὶ ἁγιοσύνης πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐξωθεῖν τοῦ εἶναι συνδημιουργὸν τοῦ θεοῦ ὅσιον. καὶ ποῖα δὲ εἰς τοῦτο μείζων ἀπόδειξις ἂν εὑρεθείη τοῦ ἐφ' ἑκάστης ἐν τῷ βαπτίσματι ἀνακαινίζειν καὶ ἁγιάζειν τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ 70 θεοῦ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ κρεῖττον καὶ πρῶτον ἀνακαλεῖσθαι σχῆμα τοῦ βίου; τοῦτο γὰρ δηλοῖ καὶ τὸ συμμνημονεύεσθαι αὐτό, ὡς τὸν ἀπόστολον περὶ τῶν ἐκ παλιγγενεσίας ἀρτίων γενέσθαι καὶ τοῦ παρὰ πάντα μεγίστου κατορθώματος ἀπολαῦσαι προσδοκωμένων ἀναφωνεῖν· «ὅπως γένησθε κατ' εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος ὑμᾶς;» προφητεύειν δὲ καὶ τὸν ∆αυὶδ ἐν ραʹ ψαλμῷ· «λαὸς ὁ κτιζόμενος αἰνέσει τὸν κύριον.» εἰ μηδὲ κοινωνίαν οὐσίας καὶ κυριότητος καὶ ἐνεργείας εἶχεν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα καὶ πρὸς τὸν· «δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα ἐγένετο» υἱόν, οὐκ ἂν ἀνακαίνιζεν καὶ ἡγίαζεν. διὸ σὺν τῷ παναγίῳ πνεύματι ὁ Χριστὸς μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν τὸν φθαρέντα τῇ παρακοῇ ἄνθρωπον ἀνακτίζων καὶ ἁγιάζων ἐνέφυσα εἰς τὰ πρόσωπα τῶν μαθητῶν καὶ ἔλεγεν· «λάβετε πνεῦμα ἅγιον·» πληρῶν τοῦ Ναοὺμ προφητείαν τὴν ὑπὸ ἀκατασχέτου πόθου τοῦ πρὸς τὸ ἄμετρον καλὸν τοῦ πράγματος τὸ γενησόμενον ὡς ἤδη πραττόμενον διηγουμένην· «ἀνέβη ἐκ τῆς γῆς ὁ ἐμφυσῶν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπόν σου, καὶ ἐξαιρούμενός σε ἐκ θλίψεως.» ὅτι δὲ κτίσαι ἐστὶν καὶ τὸ ἁγιάσαι, ὅπερ ποιεῖν πέφυκεν τὸ θεϊκὸν πνεῦμα, ∆αυὶδ μαρτυρεῖ, ψάλλων· «καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ θεός,» τουτέστιν· ἁγίασόν με, ἵν' ἀνακαινισθείην, καταφθαρεὶς τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ· ἐπεὶ πῶς ἂν αὐτῷ ἑτέρα ἐκτίσθη καρδία; συμφράζει τε τούτῳ· «καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου,» ἀντὶ τοῦ· τὸ πάντα ὑπερφέρον σεβάσμιόν σου πνεῦμα παράσχου μοι, ἵνα, φησίν, τῷ ἁγιασμῷ αὐτοῦ καθαρὸς ἀναφανείς, γένωμαι ναὸς αὐτοῦ ἄξιος. ἐκ γὰρ δὴ μόνης τῆς αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ σου ἐπιστασίας καὶ αὐτός, δέσποτα, κατασημαίνῃ ἡμῖν καὶ πάντων ἄκος δεχόμεθα κακῶν καὶ ἐν ἐλπίσιν βεβαίαις παντὸς αἰωνίου γινόμεθα ἀγαθοῦ. ἐμφανὲς γὰρ ἡμῖν, ὅτι ∆αυὶδ αὐτὸ ἐξαιτεῖ ἐγκαινισθῆναι αὐτῷ· ἐπεὶ πῶς ἂν τὸ ἤδη ὂν αὐτῷ πνεῦμα ὡς ἄρτι ἐπ' αὐτὸν ἐρχόμενον ἐνεκαινίζετο; ἀλλὰ καὶ μεῖζον καὶ ἀναγκαιότερον τὸ ἁγιάσαι τοῦ δημιουργῆσαι εἰδυῖα ἡ γραφὴ περὶ τοῦ ἀπολέσαντος τὸν ἁγιασμὸν ἐλεεινοῦ Ἰούδα εἶπεν· «καλὸν ἦν αὐτῷ, εἰ οὐκ ἐγεννήθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος,» ἐπειδή, φησίν, ἁπάντων ἀσυμφορώτατον ἔπραξεν καὶ τὸν δεσπότην ἀντ' οὐδενὸς κακοῦ ἀπέδοτο καὶ τὴν ζωὴν ἀργυρίων ἠλλάξατο. καὶ δὴ καὶ περὶ τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀρρήτῳ οἰκονομίᾳ δουλικῆς μορφῆς, περὶ ἧς λέγει Ἰωάννης μέν· «καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο,» Παῦλος δέ· «ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν, μορφὴν δούλου λαβών,» ὁ μὲν Σολομὼν εἶπεν· «ἡ σοφία ᾠκοδόμησεν ἑαυτῇ οἶκον» ὁ δὲ Ματθαῖος διὰ τὸ ταὐτὸν τῆς θεϊκῆς φύσεως καὶ ἐνεργείας ἐξέθετο ὡδί· «τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἡ γέννησις οὕτως ἦν· μνηστευθείσης τῆς μη τρὸς αὐτοῦ Μαρίας τῷ Ἰωσήφ, πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτούς, εὑρέθη ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου.» καὶ ὁ ἀρχάγγελος δὲ ἔφη· «τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου,» καὶ πάλιν· «πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐλεύσεται ἐπὶ σέ, καὶ δύναμις ὑψίστου ἑπισκιάσει σοι· διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἅγιον υἱὸς ὑψίστου κληθήσεται.» μνημονευτέον οὖν, ὅτι διὰ τὰς αἱρετικὰς ἀδολεσχίας γένεσιν προανέταξεν τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως ὁ εὐαγγελίστης, εἶτα γέννησιν. διασυρόντες γὰρ ἡμῶν τὰς γραφικὰς ἀποδείξεις, λέγουσιν πευστικῶς καθ' ὑπόκρισιν· υἱὸς οὖν τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός; πιστῶς οὐδὲ ταῦτα ἀκούοντες οὐδὲ τὸ παρ' αὐτοῦ τοῖς ἀποστόλοις εἰρημένον· «οὐκ οἴδατε, οἵου πνεύματός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.» εἰ οὖν, ἐπειδὴ ὁ πατὴρ θεὸς ἀληθινός, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡ ἐνέργεια αὐτοῦ θεῖά ἐστιν πάντη τε καὶ πάντως· ἐπειδὴ ταύτῃ ἴση καὶ ὁμοία ἡ ἐνέργεια τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος φαίνεται, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ αὐτὸ θεὸς ἀληθινὸς τυγχάνει. πρέποι δὲ ἂν καὶ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ ὡσαύτως εἰπεῖν. ἐπεὶ μή γε εἰ ἡ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐνέργεια τῆς τοῦ υἱοῦ ἢ τοῦ πνεύματος ἀμείνων, τί γὰρ καὶ ὅλως ἐνήργει τὸ πνεῦμα ἢ ὁ υἱὸς εἰς ἡμᾶς; καίτοι τὴν χείρω ἐπάγοντες δύναμιν, εἴπερ ἀνομοίως ἔχουσιν, ὡς οἱ αἱρετικοί φασιν; εἰ δὲ δὴ χρήσιμος καὶ σωτηριώδης ἡ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος πλήρωσις, κατ' οὐδὲν ἔσται ἀνόμοιος ὁ
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: ... how then is the divine Spirit not beginningless ..., the one at the very moment of the] coming to be of heaven, earth, sea being borne upon the water and making it life-engendering and life-nourishing? For just as because of saying in Job about the Son: 'the one who stretched out the heaven alone', it does not remove from the creation the Father, from whom all things and in whom all things have held together — for how then could these things be true? — so neither [is it] holy to thrust the Spirit of God, of wisdom and power and holiness, from being fellow-creator of God. And what greater proof for this could be found than the Spirit of God [page number 70, debris] on each [day] in baptism renewing and sanctifying and calling back to the better and first form of life? For the fact that it is mentioned together also shows this, so that the apostle, about those expected to become complete out of the rebirth and to enjoy the achievement greatest beyond all, cries out: 'that you may become according to the image of the one who created you'; and David too prophesies in the 101st psalm (LXX; English 102): 'a people being created will praise the Lord.' If it did not have fellowship of essence and lordship and working with the Father and with the Son 'through whom all things came to be', it would not renew and sanctify. Wherefore with the all-holy Spirit Christ after the resurrection, re-creating and sanctifying the man ruined by the disobedience, breathed into the faces of the disciples and said: 'receive Holy Spirit', fulfilling the prophecy of Nahum which, under an irrepressible longing toward the measureless beauty of the matter, relates what was going to be as already being done: 'the one breathing into your face went up from the earth, and rescuing you from affliction.' And that to sanctify too is to create, which the divine Spirit by nature does, David testifies, singing: 'create a clean heart in me, O God', that is: sanctify me, that I may be renewed, having been ruined by sin; since how could another heart be created for him? And he joins to this: 'and renew a right spirit in my inward parts', in place of: grant me your venerable Spirit surpassing all things, so that, he says, having appeared pure by its sanctification, I may become its worthy temple. For from the oversight of it alone and of your Son, you yourself also, Master, seal us, and we receive cure of all evils, and come to be in firm hopes of every eternal good. For it is evident to us that David asks for it to be renewed for him; since how could the spirit already being in him be renewed as just now coming upon him? But also the Scripture, knowing that to sanctify is greater and more necessary than to create, said about the pitiable Judas, who lost the sanctification: 'it was good for him if that man had not been born', since, it says, he did the most unprofitable of all things and sold the Master in return for no evil and exchanged the life for silver pieces. And indeed also about the slave's form in the unspeakable dispensation, about which John says: 'and the Word became flesh', and Paul: 'he emptied himself, having taken a slave's form', Solomon said: 'Wisdom built for herself a house', and Matthew, because of the sameness of the divine nature and working, set out thus: 'and the birth of Jesus Christ was thus: his mother [the word split across a line] Mary having been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found having in womb from Holy Spirit.' And the archangel said: 'for what was begotten in her is from Holy Spirit', and again: 'Holy Spirit will come upon you, and power of the Most High will overshadow you; wherefore also the holy thing being born will be called Son of the Most High.' It must be remembered, then, that because of the heretical idle-chatterings the evangelist set before the coming-into-being of the incarnation, then the birth. For, disparaging our scriptural proofs, they say in question form in pretence: is Christ then son of the Spirit? Hearing faithfully neither these things nor what was said by him to the apostles: 'you do not know of what sort of spirit the Son of Man is.' If then, since the Father is true God, because of this also his working is divine in every way and altogether, since equal and like to this the working of the Holy Spirit appears, because of this it too happens to be true God. And it would be fitting to say likewise about the Son too. Since surely not: if the working of the Father is better than that of the Son or of the Spirit, why at all would the Spirit or the Son work on us, and that bringing the worse power, if indeed they are unlike, as the heretics say? But if the fulfilment of the Son and of the Spirit is useful and saving, in no respect will be unlike the [continues in the next section: ... Son or the Spirit] ...
pass_b_english: …coming into being of heaven, earth and sea, was borne upon the water and made it bring forth and nourish life (Genesis 1:2)? For just as Job’s saying about the Son, “who alone stretched out the heaven” (Job 9:8), does not shut out from the work of creation the Father, from whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6) and in whom all things hold together (Colossians 1:17), for how else could these words still be true? So neither is it holy to thrust the Spirit of God, the Spirit of wisdom and power and holiness, out of being fellow-creator with God.

And what greater proof of this could be found than that the Spirit of God, day by day, in baptism renews and sanctifies, and calls us back to the better and first pattern of life? This is shown too by its being named in the same breath as creating: so the apostle, speaking of those who are expected to be made whole by the new birth and to enjoy the achievement greatest of all, cries out: “that you may become according to the image of him who created you” (Colossians 3:10); and David too prophesies in the hundred and second Psalm: “A people being created shall praise the Lord” (Psalm 102:18). If the Spirit had no fellowship of essence, of lordship and of working with the Father and with the Son, “through whom all things came to be” (John 1:3), he would not renew and sanctify.

That is why Christ, after the resurrection, re-creating and sanctifying with the all-holy Spirit the man who had been ruined by disobedience, breathed into the faces of the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). So he fulfilled the prophecy of Nahum, which, out of an irrepressible longing for the boundless beauty of the event, tells what was still to come as if it were already being done: “He who breathes into your face has gone up from the earth, and he rescues you from affliction” (Nahum 2:1).

That to sanctify, which the divine Spirit by nature does, is also to create, David testifies when he sings: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10); that is, sanctify me, so that I may be renewed, ruined as I am by sin. For how else could another heart have been created for him? And he joins to this: “And renew a right spirit in my inmost parts” (Psalm 51:10). This stands for: grant me your venerable Spirit, who surpasses all things, so that, he says, made pure and shown so by his sanctification, I may become his worthy temple. For only through the oversight of him and of your Son do you yourself, Master, set your seal upon us; and we receive a remedy for all evils, and come to stand in sure hopes of every eternal good. It is plain to us, then, that David asks for this Spirit to be renewed in him; otherwise how could the spirit he already had be renewed as though it were only now coming upon him?

Scripture, moreover, knowing that to sanctify is greater and more needful than to create, said of pitiable Judas, who lost his sanctification: “It would have been good for that man if he had not been born” (Matthew 26:24); because, it says, he did the most ruinous thing of all: he sold his Master, who had done him no wrong, and bartered life for pieces of silver.

And indeed, concerning the form of the servant in the ineffable dispensation, of which John says, “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and Paul, “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7): Solomon said, “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1), and Matthew, because the divine nature and working are the same, set it out thus: “Now the birth of Jesus Christ was in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:18). The archangel too said: “For what has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20); and again: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one to be born will be called Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:35).

We must remember, then, that because of the idle talk of the heretics the evangelist set the ‘coming into being’ of the incarnation first, and then the ‘birth’. For they disparage our proofs from Scripture and ask, in mock inquiry: “Is Christ, then, the son of the Spirit?” They hear with faith neither these words nor what he said to the apostles: “You do not know of what spirit the Son of Man is” (Luke 9:55).

If, then, because the Father is true God, his working is for that reason divine in every way and altogether, then, since the working of the Holy Spirit is seen to be equal and like to his, for that reason the Spirit too is true God. And it would be fitting to say the same of the Son. Otherwise, if the Father’s working were better than the Son’s or the Spirit’s, why would the Spirit or the Son work upon us at all, bringing the inferior power, if indeed they are unlike him, as the heretics say? But if the fulfilment brought by the Son and the Spirit is useful and saving, then unlike in no respect will be the …

choices.issue: Garbled draft, reversed argument, abbreviated and wrong references
choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u17): retranslated. The old English made the opening a garbled question ('To produce heaven, earth, and sea brought forth upon the water ... is his work?'), turned οὐκ ἀφιστᾷ ... τῆς δημιουργίας into 'the Father ... does not depart from creation' and ἐξωθεῖν ... ὅσιον into 'drive out the Spirit ... to be a co-creator of God, a holy one', made the Spirit the thing renewed in baptism, read ἄκος as 'sound', ἐλεεινοῦ as 'the merciful one', ἀντ' οὐδενὸς κακοῦ as 'for nothing', διασυρόντες as 'dragging through the ground', χείρω as 'a power that acts by hand', and reversed ἀμείνων ('not inferior'). It split one sentence across paragraphs ('We become for all eternal good'). References: (Matt 1:18-25) -> (Matthew 1:18), since only verse 18 is quoted; (Ps 51:10), (Jn 1:14), (Phil 2:7), (Prov 9:1) written in full; (Genesis 1:2), (1 Corinthians 8:6), (Colossians 1:17) added. Bracket '[one]' removed.

choices.term: γενέσθαι οὐρανόν, γῆν, θάλατταν ἐπιφερόμενον ἐπὶ τοῦ ὕδατος
choices.english: …coming into being of heaven, earth and sea, was borne upon the water
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence; the previous section ends 'he, at the very moment of the …' (τὸ παραυτίκα τοῦ). Only the words this section holds are translated; the question closes here.

choices.english: was borne upon the water (Genesis 1:2)
choices.why: The wording of Greek Genesis 1:2 (ἐπεφέρετο ἐπάνω τοῦ ὕδατος); cited as a clear allusion.

choices.term: διὰ τὸ λέγειν ἐν τῷ Ἰὼβ ... οὐκ ἀφιστᾷ
choices.english: Job’s saying ... does not shut out
choices.why: The articular infinitive is taken as the subject of ἀφιστᾷ; Didymus reads Job 9:8 as said of the Son.

choices.term: τὸν ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα καὶ ἐν ᾧ πάντα συνέστηκεν πατέρα
choices.english: the Father, from whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6) and in whom all things hold together (Colossians 1:17)
choices.why: Two Pauline phrases, applied here to the Father; cited by their wording.

choices.english: day by day
choices.why: Elliptic feminine; read as ἐφ' ἑκάστης ἡμέρας. 'In each one' (old English) is also possible (ψυχῆς); see problems.

choices.english: its being named in the same breath as creating
choices.why: The Greek says only 'its being mentioned together'. The two proofs that follow (Colossians 3:10, Psalm 102:18) name renewal in the language of creating, so 'as creating' is supplied from them as plain English rather than as a bracket.

choices.english: the hundred and second Psalm (Psalm 102:18)
choices.why: Greek Psalm 101 = English 102; checked by verse text.

choices.english: breathed into
choices.why: Copy-text misprint for ἐνεφύσα / ἐνεφύσησεν (John 20:22).

choices.term: Ναοὺμ ... «ἀνέβη ἐκ τῆς γῆς ὁ ἐμφυσῶν»
choices.english: (Nahum 2:1)
choices.why: Greek Nahum 2:2 (Rahlfs) = English 2:1; the KJV verse has 'he that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face', where the Greek translator read 'he who breathes'. The verse is the same; the reference uses English numbering.

choices.term: καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον / πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον
choices.english: (Psalm 51:10) twice
choices.why: Greek Psalm 50:12 = English 51:10; both halves of the verse are quoted separately.

choices.english: This stands for
choices.why: Didymus' paraphrase of the prayer follows; it is not quoted, so no quotation marks.

choices.term: ἐκ γὰρ δὴ μόνης τῆς αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ σου ἐπιστασίας καὶ αὐτός, δέσποτα, κατασημαίνῃ ἡμῖν
choices.english: For only through the oversight of him and of your Son do you yourself, Master, set your seal upon us
choices.why: The paraphrase continues in David's voice to God; κατασημαίνῃ is second person middle, 'you mark, seal'.

choices.english: It is plain to us, then
choices.why: γάρ resumes the argument after the paraphrase; αὐτὸ is the Spirit just named.

choices.english: who had done him no wrong
choices.why: 'In return for no evil': the Master had done Judas no harm.

choices.english: the form of the servant / the form of a servant
choices.why: The familiar wording of Philippians 2:7.

choices.english: The archangel
choices.why: Didymus gives both sayings to the archangel; Matthew 1:20 has 'an angel of the Lord'. Kept as he wrote it.

choices.term: γένεσιν προανέταξεν τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως ... εἶτα γέννησιν
choices.english: set the ‘coming into being’ of the incarnation first, and then the ‘birth’
choices.why: γένεσις and γέννησις are distinguished; single quotation marks show they are terms, not Scripture quotations. See problems.

choices.english: in mock inquiry
choices.why: πευστικῶς καθ' ὑπόκρισιν: a question asked in pretence.

choices.english: Otherwise, if the Father’s working were better
choices.why: The old English reversed it ('not inferior'); ἀμείνων is 'better'.

choices.english: then unlike in no respect will be the …
choices.why: The sentence runs into the next section (υἱὸς ἢ τὸ πνεῦμα); the Greek order is kept so that only the words held here are translated, ending with '…'.

choices.english: page debris
choices.why: 70 is a printed page number, skipped; μη τρὸς is one word split across a printed line.
